lines.text: אב 3 אבל
Once in Gen. 17, 4. 5, the form אַב stands
alone, in order to render the etymology
of אַבְרָהָם more distinct and obvious.
אַב Chald. m. c. suff. 1 pers. אַבִי; אֲבוּךְ,
אֲבוּהִי; plur. אֲבָהָן, the letter ה being
inserted (comp. אֲמָה), father, i. q. Heb.
אָב, Dan. 2, 23. Ezra 4, 15. 5, 12. Perh.
for grandfather, Dan. 5, 2.
אֵב m. (r. אָבַב) greenness, green, ver-
dure, of a plant. Job 8, 12 עֹדֶנּוּ בְאִבּוֹ
while yet in its greenness, i. e. yet green
and flourishing. Cant. 6, 11 אִבֵּי הַנַּחַל
the greens (green things) of the valley;
Vulg. poma, after the Chaldee usage.
Arab. أبٌّ green fodder.
אֵב Chald. (r. אֲבַב) fruit, c. suff. אִנְבֵּהּ,
the Dag. forte being resolved into Nun,
Dan. 4, 9. 11. 18. In Targg. often for פֵּרִי.
* אֲבַב in Heb. not used; Chald. Pa.
אַבֵּב to bear fruit, espec. early ripe, pre-
cocious fruit. Syr. ܗܰܒܶܒ to blossom. In
Arab. and Heb. it seems to have signifi-
ed to be green, verdant, to sprout, etc. see
the deriv. אֵב greenness, אָבִיב green ear.
The primary idea would seem to be that
of protruding, sprouting with impetus,
comp. Engl. to burst forth, to shoot,
Germ. treiben, whence אֵב pr. young
shoots; so as to have affinity with the
roots אָבָה, יָאַב, אָהַב, which express de-
sire, eager impulse; see אָהַב.
אֲבַגְתָא Abagtha, Pers. pr. n. of a eu-
nuch of Xerxes, Esth. 1, 10.—It seems to
be i. q. בִּגְתָא, and may be explained from
the Sanscr. bagadâta ‘ a fortuna datus’;
from baga fortune, the sun. (Bohlen.)
* אָבַד fut. יֹאבַד, and at the end of a
clause יֹאבֵד.
1. Prop. to lose oneself, to be lost, to
wander about, espec. of a sheep wander-
ing from the flock and lost; Arab. أَبَدَ to
flee away wild into the desert, to lose
oneself in the waste. So שֶׂה אֹבֵד a sheep
lost and wandering, Ps. 119, 176; comp.
Jer. 50, 6. Ez. 34, 4. 16. Of men, Is.
27, 13 הָאֹבְדִים בְּאֶרֶץ אַשּׁוּר who are lost
in the land of Assyria, i. e. wander as
exiles. Deut. 26, 5 אֲרַמִּי אֹבֵד a wander-
ing Syrian. Also of things, e. g. of
streams which lose themselves in the
desert, Job 6, 18. Metaph. of wisdom
become extinct, Is. 29, 14.—Hence
2. to perish, to be destroyed; Syr.
Samar. id. The Arabic in this sense
has the kindr. بَادَ. Spoken of persons
and other living things as perishing, Ps.
37, 20. Job 4, 11; sometimes with מֵעַל
Also of a land or houses which are laid
waste, Jer. 9, 11. Am. 3, 15. Metaph. of
hope, desires, vows, as failing, being dis-
appointed, Ps. 9, 19. 112, 10. Prov. 10, 28.
11, 7. Ez..12, 22.—Constr. with לְ of pers.
1 Sam. 9, 3. 20; seq. מִן Deut. 22, 3. Job
11, 20 מָנוֹס אָבַד מִנְהֶם their refuge per-
תּוֹרָה תֹּאבַד מִכֹּהֵן וְעֵצָה מִזְּקֵנִים the law
shall perish from the priest and counsel
from the aged, i. e. shall forsake them,
comp. Jer. 18, 18. 49, 7. Hence Deut.
32, 28 גּוֹי אֹבַד עֵצוֹת a nation whose
counsel is perished, void of counsel, Vulg.
consilii expers. Jer. 4, 9 יֹאבַד לֵב הַמֶּלֶךְ
the heart of the king shall perish, i. e. for
fear and terror. Job 8, 13 וְתִקְוַת חָנֵף
תֹּאבֵד and [so] shall the hope of the im-
pious man perish. Ps. 9, 19. 112, 10.
3. to be ready to perish, i. e. to be
wretched, miserable. Part. אֹבֵד one
wretched, miserable, unfortunate, Job
Piel אִבַּד 1. to lose, pr. to let be lost,
to give up as lost, Ecc. 3, 6.
2. to make wander, to scatter a flock,
3. to cause to perish, to destroy; Ecc.
7, 7 יְאַבֵּד אֶת־לֵב מַתָּנָה a gift destroyeth
i. e. corrupteth the mind. Seq. מִן, to de-
stroy out of any thing, Jer. 51, 55.—Spec.
a) Of things, to destroy, to lay waste, 2 K.
to waste one’s substance, Prov. 29, 3. b)
Of men, to destroy, to kill, to put to death,
Hiph. הֶאֱבִיד i. q. Pi. to destroy, to cut
off, as men and nations; Deut. 7, 10. 8, 20;
sometimes with the addition of מִקֶּרֶב הָעָם
Lev. 23, 30; מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם Deut. 7, 24;
also of a land, to lay waste, Zeph. 2, 5;
of hope, Job 14, 19.—Very rarely the
quiescent א in 1 pers. fut. is dropped, as
אֹבִידָה for אַאֲבִידָה Jer. 46, 8.
Deriv. אֲבֵד—אָבְדָן.

line_status.note: The third letter of the right-hand catchword has an ascender rising above the x-height of א and ב — a lamed, not a dalet (which would be flush with the top line). Running head reads אב 3 אבל.

Under the aleph of אֲמָה the print shows a composite hataf-patah (shewa dots plus a short horizontal stroke, matching the hataf under the aleph of אֲבָהָן on the line above), not a T-shaped qamets; so Reading B is correct.
Over the bāʾ the print stacks a shadda with a dammatan (nominative indefinite ending, "abbun"), not a bare shadda; over the alif only the hamza is printed, no fatḥa. That matches Reading B.

The two dots under the dageshed pe are printed side by side (tsere), not stacked vertically (shewa); the Targumic form is פֵּרִי. Everything else on the line is the same in both readings and matches the print.

Under the aleph the print shows two vertical dots plus a short horizontal stroke — a hataf patah (אֲ), not a qamets; matches the root as printed in line 1 "(r. אֲבַב)". Bet carries patah; final bet unpointed.

The vowel under the aleph is a horizontal bar, not a single dot, so it is pataḥ (Chaldee Pael אַבֵּב), not ḥireq as in B. There is a faint speck beneath the bar that could hint at a qameṣ stem, but it is far fainter than the bar and reads as ink noise; the bet has dagesh and ṣere, final bet plain, as both readings agree.
Final Arabic letter is a baseline dāl with fatha (no descending lām bowl): أَبَدَ, the expected cognate of אָבַד. Reading A is correct.

The final Arabic letter is a dāl (د) with fatḥa, not kāf — there is no inner hamza-like stroke that a final kāf (ك) carries, and the shape is the short angular hook of dāl. بَادَ "to perish" is also the expected cognate of אָבַד. Reading A is correct.

After "Ez" the print shows two baseline dots running straight into "12" with no space ("Ez..12"), as in Reading A; Reading B normalises this to a single period plus space. The Hebrew is לְ (lamed + shewa) in both, which matches the print.
The only difference is the dagesh in the tav of תֹּאבַד; the printed tav shows a dot inside it (as in תּוֹרָה beside it), so the dagesh is printed — Reading B is correct.
The verb begins with a single yod carrying sheva (יְאַבֵּד); there is no preceding vav as in Reading A.
After "nations" the print shows a semicolon (dot visible above the comma), not a comma; Reading B is correct.

Under the aleph of the first (rightmost) word the print shows a hataf-pathah (two dots plus a stroke) and there is no holem dot above the aleph, so אֲבֵד (Reading B), not אֹבֵד. Order (אֲבֵד first, then אָבְדָן) and the remaining points agree in both readings.
